## Methods

Plants, insects, cells, and antibodies
CLas-infected sweet orange (Citrus sinensis) plants were prepared through bud grafting using CLas-infected buds collected from Ningde City, Fujian Province, China. The grafted plants were maintained in a greenhouse for 3 months, after which CLas infection status was confirmed by RT-PCR analysis targeting the bacterial 16S rRNA gene.

The Asian citrus psyllid population, originally collected from CLas-free Citrus sinensis trees in Ningde City, was reared in a controlled greenhouse chamber at 27 ± 1°C with 75 ± 5% relative humidity under a 16h light/8h dark photoperiod. Newly emerged adult psyllids were allowed to feed on CLas-infected Citrus sinensis trees for 7 days before being transferred to healthy citrus plants. CLas acquisition in psyllids was verified by qPCR at 8 days post-first access to diseased plants (padp).

Spodoptera frugiperda (Sf9) insect cells were cultured in Sf900 III medium (Gibco, 12658019) supplemented with 10% heat-inactivated fetal bovine serum (FBS; EveryGREEN, 13011-8611) at 28°C. HEK-293T human embryonic kidney cells were maintained in Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM) (Gibco, 10566016) containing 10% FBS (Gibco, 10099141C) at 37°C in a humidified 5% CO2 incubator.

Custom rabbit polyclonal antibodies against D. citri Toll8, MyD88, IKKE, NFAT, Reeler, NOS, as well as against CLas Barrel and SDE3230, were generated through antigen peptide immunization as previously described64; unless otherwise specified, all antibodies were used at a dilution of 1:1000. Commercial antibodies included: FITC-conjugated Flag antibody (Invitrogen, MA1-91878-D488, 0.5 μg/μL). rhodamine-conjugated HA antibody (Invitrogen, 26183-A555, 0.5 μg/μL), β-Tubulin (TransGen Biotech, HC101, 1:5000 dilution), GAPDH (TransGen Biotech, HC301, 1:3000 dilution), Myc Tag (TransGen Biotech, HT101, 1:3000 dilution), Flag Tag (TransGen Biotech, HT201, 1:3000 dilution), HA Tag (TransGen Biotech, HT301, 1:3000 dilution), His Tag (TransGen Biotech, HT501, 1:3000 dilution) and GST Tag (TransGen Biotech, HT601, 1:3000 dilution), phospho-IKKE (Beyotime, AF5959, 1:1000 dilution), ubiquitin (Ub; Abmart, T55520, 1:1000 dilution), Ub K48 (Abmart, T55964, 1:1000 dilution), histone H3 (Abcam, ab1791, 1:5000 dilution), and HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies (goat anti-rabbit IgG, Thermo Fisher 32460, 1: 5000 dilution; goat anti-mouse IgG, Thermo Fisher 32430, 1:5000 dilution).

RT-qPCR analysis
To quantify gene expression levels of Toll1, Toll6, Toll7, Toll8, MyD88, IKKE, NFAT, Reeler, NOS, and CLas secretory protein genes in psyllids, total RNA was extracted from 30 adult insects pooled at 8 days padp using TRIzol reagent (Invitrogen) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. First-strand cDNA synthesis was synthesized from 1 μg total RNA using RevertAid Reverse Transcriptase (Promega, EP0441) and oligo(dT) primers. RT-qPCR reactions were conducted in triplicate using the SYBR Green PCR Master Mix (GenStar, A304-10) on a QuantStudio 6 Flex Real-Time PCR System (Applied Biosystems). Relative gene expression was calculated using the 2−ΔΔCt method, with D. citri Actin or CLas 16S rRNA as endogenous controls. Primer sequences are provided in Supplementary Table 3.

Western blotting
Total proteins were extracted from 30 CLas-free or CLas-positive psyllids at 8 days padp using NP-40 lysis buffer (Beyotime, P0013F) containing protease inhibitor cocktail (Roche, 11697498001). For dimerization assays, protein samples were mixed with native loading buffer (62.5 mM Tris-HCl, pH 6.8, 25% glycerol, 0.01% bromophenol blue) and resolved on 10% non-denaturing polyacrylamide gels. Proteins were transferred to PVDF membranes (Millipore, IPFL00010), blocked with 5% non-fat milk, and probed with primary antibodies (1: 1000 dilution) overnight at 4°C. After incubation with HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies (1:5000 dilution), signals were developed using Luminata Classico Western HRP Substrate (Millipore, WBKLS0500) and imaged on a Luminescent Image Analyzer AI600 (GE Healthcare). Band intensities were quantified using ImageJ software (NIH).

Transmission electron microscopy
Midgut tissues from CLas-free or CLas-positive adult psyllid (16 days padp) were dissected and fixed in 2% (v/v) glutaraldehyde and 2% (v/v) paraformaldehyde in 0.1 M phosphate buffer (PBS; pH 7.4) for 2 h at room temperature, followed by post-fixation in 1% (w/v) osmium tetroxide for 1 h. Samples were dehydrated through an ethanol series (30–100%), embedded in Spurr’s resin (SPI Supplies, 02680-AB), and polymerized at 60°C for 72 h. Ultrathin sections (70 nm) were cut using a Leica EM UC7 ultramicrotome, mounted on nickel grids, and immunolabeled with CLas Barrel-specific IgG (0.5 μg/mL) followed by 10 nm gold-conjugated goat anti-rabbit secondary antibody (1: 100 dilution, Abcam, ab27236). Grids were counterstained with uranyl acetate and lead citrate before imaging on a Hitachi HT-7800 TEM operated at 80 kV.

Yeast two-hybrid assay
Full-length open reading frames (ORF) of Toll8, MyD88, IKKE, UBR5, Barrel, and SDE3230 (signal peptide removed) were cloned into the bait vector pGBKT7. Domain fragments and point mutants were generated as follows: IKKE: PKc domain (aa 18–332), Ubl domain (aa 310–387), TBK1 domain (aa 405–644), Q342A/E343A mutants; Toll8: LRR domain (aa 221–931), TIR domain (aa 1083–1217), N679A/N712A/D717A mutants; Toll1: LRR domain (aa 197–586), Toll6: LRR domain (aa 55–711), Toll7: LRR domain (aa 264–945); MyD88: DD domain (aa 43–121), TIR domain (aa 176–276), T103A/C110A mutant; NFAT: N-terminal (aa 1–139), RHD domain (aa 140–458), C-terminal (aa 459–1140) were cloned into pGADT7. For prey constructs, we cloned the following CLas membrane protein ORFs into pGADT7: ABCt (GenBank WP_015452444), BamA (GenBank WP_015452389), BamD (GenBank WP_015453002), Barrel (GenBank WP_015452909), CpaB (GenBank WP_015452434), EamA (GenBank WP_015452584), FliQ (GenBank WP_015452639), FlgA (GenBank WP_012778596), FliR (GenBank WP_015452647), FlhA (GenBank WP_015452646), FliF (GenBank WP_015824893), FlhB (GenBank WP_015452471), Kup (GenBank WP_015452667), LolA (GenBank WP_012778744), MotA (GenBank WP_015452475), MurJ (GenBank WP_012778749), PBP1 (GenBank WP_040055318), PBP2 (GenBank ALK07622) and YldC (GenBank WP_012778702). All recombinant constructs were sequence-verified prior to yeast transformation. Yeast strain AH109 was co-transformed with bait/prey plasmids using the LiAc/SS carrier DNA/PEG method and plated on SD/-Trp-Leu-His-Ade (QDO) medium. The pGBKT7-53/pGADT7-T interaction served as a positive control, while the pGBKT7-Lam/pGADT7-T interaction served as a negative control. Positive interactions were confirmed by colony growth after 5 days at 30°C. All plasmids were confirmed by DNA sequencing. Primer sequences are listed in Supplementary Table 3.

Glutathione S-transferase pull-down assay
GST-tagged proteins (Barrel, MyD88-TIR, UBR5, IKKE, NFAT-RHD) cloned into pGEX-4T-3 and His-tagged proteins (Toll8, Toll8 mutants, MyD88, SDE3230, IKKE-PKc) cloned into pET-28a were expressed in E. coli Rosetta (DE3) cells. GST fusion proteins were immobilized on glutathione-sepharose 4B beads (GE Healthcare, 17075601) and incubated with His-tagged proteins in binding buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl, pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl, 0.1% NP-40) for 4 h at 4°C. Beads were washed five times with ice-cold PBS, and bound proteins were eluted with 10 mM reduced glutathione. Interactions were verified by Western blot using anti-His (1:3000 dilution) and anti-GST (1:3000 dilution) antibodies. Primer sequences are listed in Supplementary Table 3.

RNA interference
The dsRNAs targeting Toll1, Toll6, Toll7, Toll8, MyD88, IKKE, NFAT, Reeler, NOS, and GFP were synthesized using the T7 RiboMAX Express RNAi system (Promega, P1700). Approximately 600 CLas-free or CLas-positive adults (8 days padp) were microinjected with 46 nL dsRNAs (1 μg/μL) using a Nanoject II Auto-Nanoliter Injector (Drummond Scientific). The dsGFP treatment served as a control. At 3 days post-injection, 30 insects per replicate were pooled for RT-qPCR and Western blot analysis. Three biological replicates were performed. Primer sequences are listed in Supplementary Table 3.

Protein microinjection assays
Recombinant CLas Barrel and SDE3230 proteins expressed in E. coli were purified using Ni-NTA affinity chromatography (Qiagen, 30210). Approximately 300 CLas-free psyllid adults were microinjected with 1 μg/μL purified protein. At 48h post-injection, 30 insects per replicate were pooled for total proteins or nuclear proteins were extracted using NP-40 lysis buffer or Nuclear/Cytoplasmic Extraction Kit (Beyotime, P0027) and analyzed by western blot. GFP protein (1 μg/μL) served as a negative control. Three biological replicates were performed.

Proteasome inhibition and NO modulation
Approximately 300 CLas-infected adults (8 days padp) were microinjected with 10 μM MG-132 (Selleckchem, S2619), 100 μM SNP (NO activator; Beyotime, S1901), or 100 μM L-NMMA (NO inhibitor; Beyotime, S0011) in PBS containing 0.1% DMSO. Control groups received PBS containing 0.1% DMSO alone. Toll8, MyD88, IKKE, NFAT, and Barrel protein levels were quantified by western blot at 24h post-treatment. Each replicate involved analyzing a pool of 30 treated insects, with three replicates conducted.

NO quantification assays
Lysates were collected from 30 psyllids per replicate for control or treatment groups, and centrifuged (10,000 × g, 10 min). NO levels in supernatants were measured using a Nitric Oxide Assay Kit (Beyotime, S0021) following the manufacturer’s protocol. Absorbance was read at 540 nm on a microplate reader (BioTek Synergy H1).

Structural modeling and molecular docking
Protein structures of Toll8, Barrel, MyD88, and IKKE were predicted using Alphafold3 (DeepMind) and validated via SAVESv6.1 (https://saves.mbi.ucla.edu/). Molecular docking was performed using GRAMM-X (http://vakser.compbio.ku.edu/resources/gramm/grammx/) with default parameters. The top-scoring complexes were analyzed using PDBePISA (https://www.ebi.ac.uk/pdbe/pisa/) and visualized in ChimeraX 1.4.

Baculovirus expression system
ORFs of target genes (Toll8, Toll8 mutants, Barrel, MyD88, MyD88 mutants, IKKE, IKKE mutants, NFAT, NFAT mutants, and Ub) were cloned into pFastBac1 with C-terminal Flag/Myc/HA tags. Recombinant bacmids were generated in E. coli DH10Bac (Thermo Fisher, 10361012) and transfected into Sf9 cells using Cellfectin II Reagent (Thermo Fisher, 10362100). Viral stocks were amplified through two passages, and protein expression was confirmed by Western blot.

Immunofluorescence microscopy
Midgut tissues from CLas-infected adults (8 days padp) were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde, permeabilized with 0.2% Triton X-100, and incubated with rhodamine-conjugated NFAT antibody (1:200 dilution) overnight at 4°C. Nuclei were counterstained with DAPI (1 μg/mL; Thermo Fisher, D1306). Images were acquired on a Leica TCS SPE confocal microscope using a 100× oil immersion objective.

Sf9 cells infected with recombinant bacmids expressing Flag-SDE3230, HA-IKKE, or Flag-NFAT were seeded on coverslips and harvested at 24 or 36 hpi. Cells were fixed, permeabilized, immunolabeled with Flag-FITC (0.5 μg/μL), HA-rhodamine (0.5 μg/μL), and DAPI (0.5 μg/μL), and processed for immunofluorescence microscopy.

Phos-tag SDS-PAGE
For phosphorylation analysis, Sf9 cells expressing Flag-NFAT (or its mutants) and HA-IKKE harvested at 48 hpi and lysed in Phos-tag lysis buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl, pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl, 1% NP-40, 1× phosphatase inhibitors [Beyotime, P1091]). Proteins were separated on 8% SDS-PAGE gels containing 50 μM Phos-tag acrylamide (Wako, 304-93521) and 100 μM MnCl2, then transferred to PVDF membranes for immunoblotting.

CLas transmission assay
To evaluate the effect of gene silencing on CLas transmission, we performed inoculation experiments using adult D. citri that had been reared for multiple generations on CLas-infected sweet orange (Citrus sinensis) plants. Given that CLas titer in psyllids is a key determinant of transmission efficiency65, we first assessed bacterial levels in the insects prior to inoculation. A random sample of 30 adult psyllids was starved for 6 h and subjected to qPCR analysis of CLas titer in head-thorax tissues. All sampled insects tested positive for CLas, with cycle threshold (Ct) values below 20, indicating a high acquisition rate and confirming successful CLas infection cycle and abundant bacterial accumulation.

Previous study showed that CLas transmission by infected psyllids feeding on young citrus leaves typically requires nearly 3 months before HLB symptoms become visible65. To expedite the assessment of CLas transmission efficiency, a method has been established in which infected psyllids are confined to young citrus leaves for a 7-day inoculation access period, followed by a 7-day accumulation phase, after which CLas can be detected by qPCR23. Based on this approach, approximately 600 CLas-infected psyllids were microinjected with 46 nL dsRNAs (1 μg/μL) targeting IKKE, NOS, Reeler, or GFP. Two days post-injection, 15 dsRNA-treated psyllids were confined onto each healthy young leaf (4–6 cm in length) from uninfected C. sinensis plants using a leaf clip cage (Supplementary Fig. 4i). The insects were allowed to feed for 7 days under controlled conditions (27°C, 14:10 L:D photoperiod)23. After the inoculation period, psyllids were removed and stored for subsequent analysis. The exposed citrus leaves were maintained in an incubator at 27°C for an additional 7 days to allow potential CLas propagation. For each treatment group, ten leaf replicates were prepared.

Total DNA was extracted from leaf vein-adjacent (midribs and major veins) tissues on which psyllids had fed, using a CTAB-based method. Given that the leaf veins are primary sites for CLas accumulation, sampling these regions provides a partial enrichment of bacterial DNA, thereby improving detection sensitivity65. Tissues were ground in liquid nitrogen and homogenized in 500 μL of pre-warmed CTAB buffer (2% CTAB, 100 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8.0, 20 mM EDTA, 1.4 M NaCl, 0.5% 2-mercaptoethanol, 1% PVP). After incubation at 65°C for 30 min, samples were extracted with an equal volume of chloroform:isoamyl alcohol (24:1). The aqueous phase was recovered, and nucleic acids were precipitated with 0.7 volumes of isopropanol, washed with 70% ethanol, and resuspended in 10 μL nuclease-free water. DNA concentration and purity were determined spectrophotometrically, and all samples were adjusted to 100 ng/μL for downstream analysis.

Quantitative PCR was performed using a SYBR Green-based system targeting the CLas 16S rDNA gene. The reaction mixture (20 μL) contained 1× SYBR Green Master Mix (GenStar, A304-10), 500 nM of each primer, and 2 μL of template DNA. Amplification was carried out on a QuantStudio 6 Flex Real-Time PCR System (Applied Biosystems) under the following conditions: 95°C for 10 min, followed by 40 cycles of 95°C for 15 s and 60°C for 45 s. Melting curve analysis was subsequently performed by increasing the temperature from 60 to 95°C at a rate of 0.5°C/s to verify amplification specificity. Each run included a standard curve generated from serial dilutions of a plasmid containing the target CLas 16S rDNA fragment and non-template controls to monitor contamination. Samples with Ct values ≤ 35 that exhibited a single specific melting peak were considered positive for CLas infection.

Three independent biological replicates were performed to ensure reproducibility. The survival rate of microinjected psyllids was >85% across all treatment groups at the conclusion of the 7-day inoculation period.

Protein dimerization and activation assays
Sf9 cells expressing His-Barrel along with Flag-Toll8 or Flag-Toll8 mutants for 48 h were lysed using NP-40 buffer containing 1 μM protease inhibitors cocktail and analyzed by 10% native PAGE or SDS-PAGE, followed by immunoblotting with the specified antibodies (1: 2000 dilution). Similarly, Sf9 cells expressing Myc-MyD88 together with His-Barrel or Flag-Toll8 for 48 h were analyzed by native PAGE and SDS-PAGE, followed by immunoblotting.

To identify critical interaction residues in MyD88 and IKKE, Sf9 cells expressing Myc-MyD88 (wild-type and mutants), HA-IKKE (wild-type and mutants), or Flag-Toll8 for 48 h were analyzed by native PAGE for MyD88 dimerization and SDS-PAGE for IKKE phosphorylation and protein expression levels.

NFAT phosphorylation analysis
For phosphorylation site identification, Flag-NFAT expressing Sf9 cells were lysed at 48 hpi, immunoprecipitated with anti-Flag magnetic beads (Beyotime, P2181), and separated by SDS-PAGE. A major band of approximately 135 kDa was excised, digested with trypsin, and analyzed by phosphorylation mass spectrometry at APTBIO (Shanghai, China). Potential target peptides were identified and analyzed using Mascot (matrixscience.com) and assembled using Geneious 9.0.2.

To determine the significance of S167 in NFAT phosphorylation, point mutations were introduced within the amino acid region 167–180. Mutant NFAT m1 retained Ser167, while NFAT m2 underwent complete mutation. Sf9 cells expressing HA-IKKE with NFAT WT, NFAT m1, or NFAT m2 were analyzed by Phos-tag SDS-PAGE.

Chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing and qPCR analysis
Chromatin from 100 CLas-free psyllids was crosslinked with 1% formaldehyde, sonicated to 200–500 bp fragments, and immunoprecipitated with an NFAT antibody (1:100 dilution) or control rabbit IgG (1:100 dilution, Beyotime, A7016) using a SimpleChIP Plus Kit (Cell Signaling, 9005)66. Libraries were sequenced on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000 (2×150 bp) by YankeGene (Guangdong, China). Reads were aligned to the D. citri genome (GCA_000475195.1) using Bowtie2, and peaks were called with MACS2 (q < 0.05). Reeler and NOS promoter enrichment was quantified by qPCR and analyzed using Student’s t-test (three biological replicates).

Yeast one-hybrid assay
The 5’ regulatory regions of Reeler and NOS genes containing putative NFAT binding sites (NFATBS) were cloned into pHis2 vector. NFAT cDNA was cloned into pGADT7 vector. Yeast strain Y187 was co-transformed with pGADT7-NFAT and pHis2-Reeler or pHis2-NOS, with appropriate controls. Transformants were selected on -His/Leu/Trp media containing 180 mM 3-Amino-1,2,4-triazole (3-AT; Coolaber, CA1311) at 30°C (three replicates). Images were captured 4 days after incubation.

Electrophoretic mobility shift assay
Flag-NFAT protein was expressed in Sf9 cells, immunoprecipitated using anti-Flag magnetic beads (Beyotime, P2181S), and eluted with 3× Flag peptide. Cy5-labeled probes (Reeler, 5′-CGGGTTTTCC-3′ or NOS, 5′-CGGCCAAACCCC-3′) and unlabeled/mutant probes (Reeler mut, 5′-CAAACCCCCC-3′ or NOS mut, TGGCCGGGTTTT-3′) were synthesized by Tsingke Technology. EMSA reactions containing 20 nmol probe, 100 μg Flag-NFAT, and 10 nmol Poly(dI-dC) were performed in EMSA buffer (10 mM Tris, pH 7.5, 0.25 mM DTT, 5 mM MgCl2, 10 mM KCl) at 4°C for 30 min. Competitive EMSA was performed by adding 20, 50, 100, and 200 nmol of unlabeled oligos 20 min prior to the addition of labeled oligos. Reactions were resolved on 5% non-denaturing PAGE gels and imaged on an Odyssey CLx Imaging System (LI-COR).

Dual-luciferase reporter assay
The ORF of the NFAT was cloned into the pcDNA3.1 vector (pcDNA-NFAT). The promoter regions of Reeler and NOS were cloned into the pGL3-Basic vector (pGL3-Reeler and pGL3-NOS). For the dual-luciferase reporter assay, HEK-293T cells were transfected with 1000 ng of reporter gene plasmids (pGL3-vector, pGL3-Reeler, or pGL3-NOS), 500 ng of pRL-TK Renilla luciferase plasmid as an internal control, and either 0, 500, or 2000 ng of pcDNA-NFAT expression plasmids using the Lipo8000 kit (Beyotime, C0533). Firefly and Renilla luciferase activities were measured 48 h post-transfection using the Dual Luciferase Reporter Assay Kit (YEASEN, 11402ES60). Each experiment was performed in triplicate.

Reeler antibacterial activity in vitro
X. citri and S. fredii were cultured in LB liquid medium at 28°C until the optical density (OD) reached 0.6. Purified Reeler protein, expressed in the E. coli Rosseta strain at a concentration of 0.5 mg/mL, was co-incubated with these two bacterial strains at room temperature. The total volume of the co-incubation mixture was 100 μL, with the induced expression product from the empty pET-28a vector serving as a control. Following the instructions of the LIVE/DEAD Bacterial Staining Kit with DMAO and PI (Beyotime, C2030S), the co-incubation products were stained. The stained bacterial suspensions were observed under an immunofluorescence microscope. Live bacteria with intact cell membranes exhibited green fluorescence, while dead bacteria with damaged cell membranes displayed both green and red fluorescence.

Protein degradation assay
The ORFs of MyD88 or UBR5 were constructed into a pcDNA3.1 plasmid. HEK-293T cells were transfected with 1000 ng of Flag-MyD88 plasmids, and either 0, 500, 1000, or 1500 ng of His-UBR5 expression plasmids using the Lipo8000 transfection kit. Total cellular proteins were extracted using RIPA lysis buffer (Beyotime, P0013) for western blot analysis.

Co-Immunoprecipitation assay
To investigate whether MyD88 undergoes ubiquitination modification in psyllids, adults were injected with 10 μM MG-132. At 6 h post-injection, total cellular proteins were extracted using NP-40 lysis buffer and incubated with magnetic beads (Beyotime, P2181) conjugated with MyD88 antibody (1:100 dilution) for 6 h at 4°C. Rabbit IgG magnetic beads (Beyotime, P2173) served as the control. Ubiquitination modification of MyD88 was detected by western blot using an Ub antibody (1:1000 dilution).

Sf9 cells expressing Flag-MyD88, HA-Ub, Myc-UBR5, or His-SDE3230 were treated with 10 μM MG-132 and lysed in NP-40 lysis buffer at 48 hpi. Cell lysates were prepared, and the substrate protein Flag-MyD88 was immunoprecipitated with anti-Flag beads (Beyotime, P2115). Ubiquitin-modified proteins were subsequently detected using western blot assays with specific antibodies (1:1000 dilution).

The UbPred software package (www.ubpred.org) was used to predict potential ubiquitination sites on the MyD88 protein. Three lysine residues were identified as potential ubiquitination sites: K48 within the death domain (DD), K201 within the Toll/interleukin-1 receptor (TIR) domain, and K301 at the C-terminus. Site-directed mutagenesis was performed to substitute K48, K201, and K301 with arginine, generating the MyD88 K48R, MyD88 K201R, and MyD88 K301R mutant proteins for ubiquitination analysis. For ubiquitination assays, Sf9 cells were co-transfected to express Flag-MyD88 (wild-type or mutants), Myc-UBR5, and HA-Ub. Cells were treated with 10 μM MG-132 for 6 h prior to harvest at 48 hpi. Cell lysates were prepared using NP-40 lysis buffer, and Flag-tagged proteins were immunoprecipitated with anti-Flag magnetic beads. Ubiquitin-modified MyD88 was detected by western blot analysis using anti-HA and anti-Ub K48 antibodies (1:1000 dilution).

In vitro ubiquitylation assay
To assess the effect of UBR5 on the ubiquitination modification of MyD88 or SDE3230 in vitro, purified 0.5 μg Ub (Aladdin, 79586-22-4), 1 μg E1 (UBA1), 2 μg E2 (UBE2D3), 5 μg HA-UBR5, 5 μg Flag-MyD88 or 5 μg Flag-SDE3230 were incubated in reaction buffer (1 M Tris, pH 7.5, 100 mM ATP, 200 mM MgCl2 and 40 mM DTT, 20×) at 30°C for 2 h. Reactions were terminated with SDS loading buffer and analyzed by Western blot.

Gene identification and phylogenetic analyses
Genes in D. citri were identified based on genome (GCA_000475195.1) and confirmed using conserved domain analysis with the NCBI Conserved Domain Database (CCD; https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/Structure/cdd). Sequences used in the phylogenetic analyses of Toll, NFAT, and IKKE are provided in Supplementary Table 4. Phylogenetic analysis and the number of PGRP and GNBP genes in D. citri were referenced from previously research57,67. Sequence alignments were generated using MAFFT with default settings. Phylogenetic trees were constructed using IQ-TREE (http://iqtree.cibiv.univie.ac.at) with default parameters and visualized using iTOL (https://itol.embl.de).

Alignment of protein 3D structures
The 3D structure of TLR2 was obtained from PDB database (https://www.rcsb.org/). The 3D structures of Toll1, Toll6, Toll7, and Toll8 were predicted using the Alphafold3 server (Google DeepMind). Structural alignments were performed using PyMOL, and the root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) values for pairwise comparisons were calculated and presented in a matrix.

Statistical data analysis
All graphs and statistical analyses were created using the GraphPad Prism version 8.0.1. Data were analyzed using a two-tailed unpaired Student’s t-test and expressed as means ± SEM. The significance level was set at P < 0.05.

This study focuses on the identification of ClBarrel, an outer membrane protein from Candidatus Liberibacter (Cl), the bacterium responsible for Huanglongbing (HLB), a devastating citrus disease. mediating pathogen defense by directly engaging Toll receptors and initiating immune

Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
This study focuses on the identification of ClBarrel, an outer membrane protein from
Candidatus Liberibacter (Cl), the bacterium responsible for Huanglongbing (HLB), a
devastating citrus disease. Cl is transmitted to plants through insects, particularly
psyllids such as Diaphorina citri, which deliver the pathogen into the plant phloem.
The bacterium disrupts assimilate transport, leading to wilting in the host plant.
However, less is understood about how the vector insects themselves recognize
bacterial surface patterns. While extensive research has explored insect innate
immune activation, particularly in Drosophila, the mechanisms by which vector
insects respond to pathogens are still poorly understood.
In this study, the authors present a rare example of direct recognition between
ClBarrel and the ectodomain of a newly identified Toll-like receptor (TLR), TLR8,
from D. citri. This discovery demonstrates that insects can activate innate immune
responses to plant pathogens that they transmit, facilitating the pathogen's journey
into host plants. Upon ligand binding, TLR8 undergoes dimerization and recruits the
co-receptor MyD88, initiating a signaling cascade. This leads to the activation of IκB
kinase IRD5, which in turn activates the transcription factor NFAT. This signaling
pathway mirrors canonical innate immune responses, and in this study, the authors
identify the D. citri homologs analogous to those found in Drosophila.
The most compelling part of this research lies in the second key finding: the bacterial
effector SDE3230. This effector is produced by Cl and functions to suppress the insect
immune response. It does so by ubiquitinating and degrading MyD88 through the
proteasome, preventing the activation of immune responses that could otherwise harm
the pathogen. This discovery highlights an intricate interplay between immune
activation and suppression as the pathogen moves from the insect vector to the plant.
As a plant immunologist, I am particularly excited by the extensive data supporting
the proposed model and the quality of the research. While I am less familiar with the
literature in insect innate immunity, based on standards in our field, this study
represents an outstanding contribution to the scientific community. I have no
significant critiques but would suggest simplifying the writing slightly to improve
accessibility for readers less familiar with the topic.
Response: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer's generous assessment of our work
and your valuable suggestion regarding accessibility. As a plant immunologist, your
perspective on broadening readership is particularly insightful. In response to your
comments, we have reorganized the Results section into three clearly defined parts
focusing on pathogen recognition, signal transduction, and immune suppression to
improve logical flow. Additionally, we have streamlined complex sentence structures
and incorporated explanatory phrases for specialized terminology where appropriate.
These modifications were carefully implemented to enhance overall readability while
maintaining scientific precision, as can be seen throughout the revised manuscript,
particularly in the Results section. We are especially grateful for your encouraging
comments about the work's significance, which have helped us strengthen the
manuscript's clarity and accessibility.
